newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says Arafat stalling deal to rally support.
newsitem.headline: Israel says Arafat stalling deal to rally support.

text.p: Israel's top negotiator with the PLO accused Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday of stalling in talks on Hebron in order to rally European and Arab support for his stand.

Israelis and Palestinians return to the bargaining table on Wednesday to try to break the deadlock over Israel's promised redeployment in the West Bank town where tension runs high between Arabs and Jews.
In the West Bank village of Husan on Wednesday, a U.S. government representative visited the family of an 11-year-old Palestinian boy allegedly killed by a Jewish settler.

"He is trying to create a support structure for himself in the Arab world and in Europe by presenting the (Palestinian) misery over the fact that the agreements have still not been implemented," said negotiator Dan Shomron, referring to Arafat's current European tour.
"Only when he decides the time has come and has played out this process in which he creates some sort of support...will he give the green light to close matters," he told Israel Radio.
Palestinians blame Israel for the impasse, accusing the Jewish state of trying to reneogiate a deal already sealed with the previous Labour government.

"It's not in the Palestinian interest to delay any agreement but the attempt to impose political and security dictations harms the Palestinian interests and that is rejected," said PLO official Hassan Asfour.

The two sides have struggled to hammer out terms for a partial Israeli withdrawal from Hebron where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Arabs. U.S. mediator Dennis Ross left for home this week after negotiators failed to seal a deal.
Hebron is the last of seven towns Israel promised to hand over to Palestinians under a 1995 Israel-PLO peace deal.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ousted Labour in elections last May, opposed the deal but has vowed to honour it once Palestinians agree to modifications that would ensure the safety of settlers in the town.
Withdrawal from Hebron, where tombs of biblical forefathers are held holy by Moslems and Jews, has been delayed since March, with frequent outbursts of violence.
Security sources said shots were fired on Wednesday at an Israeli guard post in Hebron.

Settlers shouting "Hebron is ours" shoved, cursed and spat at PLO officials who toured the city on Tuesday, Israeli and Palestinian witnesses said. On Sunday, Jewish settlers fired near Palestinians after their vehicle was pelted with stones.
Elsewhere in the West Bank, U.S. Consul-General Edward Abington paid a condolence call to the Shousha family two days after their son Hilmi died of a brain haemorrhage.
I convey my condolences and the condolences of the United States government," Abington told the family.

"I have a six-year-old and she is the most precious thing that I have and if anything happened to her it would be devasting to me, so I know the Shousha family must be heartbroken at the death of their son," he said.
Hilmi Shousha died in an Israeli hospital on Monday a day after the security chief of a Jewish settlement adjacent to Husan beat him on the head with a pistol butt and stomped on him, villagers said.
The settler, Nahum Kurman, has been in police custody since Sunday, refusing to answer questions by investigators.

Other settlers say Kurman chased Hilmi after he threw stones at Israeli vehicles but did not beat the boy. An autopsy showed Shousha died from bleeding in the brain caused by a sharp blow to the neck.
